To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

blind people have a different set of gesture preferences from sighted people, that blind people have difficulty performing gestures that require fine motor control or precision, and that blind people have an increased preference for gestures that involve tapping on a keyboard.

(1) blind people prefer edge-based gestures and virtual key gestures to center-based gestures and (2) blind people perform edge-based gestures and key gestures more quickly, with larger and more variable gesture sizes, and with more variable gesture shapes than sighted people.
blind people prefer gestures that use edge gestures and tapping on virtual keyboards, and that they perform these gestures differently from sighted people.

the design of touch screens for the visually impaired.
the design of touch screen interfaces that are both usable and accessible to blind people.
the question of whether and to what extent blind and sighted people gesture in similar ways.

we have found that blind people and sight people use gestures differently and we can design interfaces for blind people based on their gestures.
the results suggest new design guideline for accessible touch screen interface.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
blind people use gestures differently from sighted people, and that these differences should be taken into consideration in the design of accessible touch screen interfaces.
blind people have a preference for edge-based gestures, gestures that involve tapping keys on a virtual keyboard, and gestures that use the entire screen.

the design of touch screen gestures for blind people should focus on the use of the screen edges and on the use of virtual keyboard-like gestures.
